Roth Conversions:
Tax Now, Not Later

lines.text: This Roth move has had no income limit since 2010.
lines.say: This Roth move has had no income limit since twenty ten.

lines.text: It's a Roth conversion: move pre-tax IRA money into a Roth and pay the tax now.
lines.say: It's a Roth conversion: move pre-tax IRA money into a Roth and pay the tax now.

lines.text: In 2010, conversions jumped over 800%, to $64.8 billion.
lines.say: In twenty ten, conversions jumped over eight hundred percent, to sixty-four point eight billion dollars.

lines.text: The catch: what you convert counts as ordinary income that year.
lines.say: The catch: what you convert counts as ordinary income that year.

lines.text: Example: 2026, single, federal only, all in one bracket. Converting $10,000 costs $1,200 at 12%, $2,200 at 22%.
lines.say: Example: twenty twenty-six, single, federal only, all in one bracket. Converting ten thousand costs twelve hundred at twelve percent, twenty-two hundred at twenty-two percent.

lines.text: It's a bet on your tax rate: higher later, paying now usually wins; lower later, it usually costs you.
lines.say: It's a bet on your tax rate: higher later, paying now usually wins; lower later, it usually costs you.

lines.text: Fine print: it must be done by Dec 31, with no undo since 2018.
lines.say: Fine print: it must be done by December thirty-first, with no undo since twenty eighteen.

lines.text: Under 59½, withdrawing converted money within 5 years of that conversion can trigger a 10% extra tax.
lines.say: Under fifty-nine and a half, withdrawing converted money within five years of that conversion can trigger a ten percent extra tax.

post.title: This Roth move has had no income limit since 2010
post.ig:
This Roth move has had no income limit since 2010.
A Roth conversion moves pre-tax IRA money into a Roth; the converted amount counts as ordinary income that year.
When the income cap ended in 2010, conversions rose over 800% to $64.8B (IRS SOI).
Example, 2026 single filer, federal only, all in one bracket: converting $10,000 costs $1,200 in the 12% bracket vs $2,200 in the 22% bracket.
Fine print: done by Dec 31 to count for the year, no recharacterization since 2018, and under 59½, withdrawing converted money within 5 years of each conversion can trigger a 10% extra tax.
Sources: IRS Rev. Proc. 2025-32, IRS Topic 309, IRS Pub 590-B, IRS SOI Bulletin Fall 2013.
